title: ConQUESTA: Topology-Aware Post-Training Structural Pruning of Quantum Neural Networks
abstract: Deploying quantum neural networks (QNNs) on sparse hardware requires preserving task accuracy while reducing compiler-induced two-qubit gates, SWAPs, and depth. We present ConQUESTA (\underline{C}onstrained \underline{Qu}antum \underline{E}ntangler \underline{S}election with \underline{T}opology \underline{A}wareness), a post training pruning framework that combines task saliency with compiler cost, screens candidate entanglers, and searches complete pruning masks under an explicit accuracy constraint. Unlike one-shot ranking, each mask is transpiled as a whole across multiple coupling topologies. Across 4-, 6-, and 8-qubit QNNs and eight model seeds at 55% pruning, ConQUESTA achieves mean resource reductions of 61.6% on Breast Cancer, 72.0% on Digits01, and 82.2% on Iris, exceeding the strongest matched simple baseline by 3.5, 1.7, and 8.9 percentage points, respectively. Fixed-mask recovery raises feasibility from 16/24 to 22/24 runs. In a fixed-k=4 scaling study on a scaling probe of 4 to 12-qubits, the raw mask space grew from 495 to 12.1M while the evaluated masks increase only from 189 to 305. Resource-weight changes alter depth/routing priorities with at most a 0.44-point mean validation shift.
summary: This paper presents ConQUESTA, a novel post-training pruning framework designed to optimize Quantum Neural Networks for deployment on sparse quantum hardware. By combining task performance metrics with compiler-specific hardware costs, ConQUESTA significantly reduces resource requirements like two-qubit gates and circuit depth. This work provides a practical tool for making QNNs more viable for real-world quantum computation.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of deploying Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) on hardware with limited connectivity by developing a method to prune the network structure.
main_result: ConQUESTA achieves significant mean resource reductions (up to 82.2% on Iris) compared to simple baselines, demonstrating superior physical efficiency while maintaining high task accuracy.
method: It introduces ConQUESTA, a post-training pruning framework that jointly optimizes for task saliency and compiler-induced hardware costs by searching complete pruning masks across multiple coupling topologies.
model_or_system: The model is a Quantum Neural Network (QNN) implemented via Parameterized Quantum Circuits (PQCs), tested across various qubit counts (4 to 12) and benchmark datasets (Breast Cancer, Digits01, Iris).
key_observables: Resource reductions (two-qubit gates, SWAPs, circuit depth), Validation Accuracy, and Feasibility rates.
important_parameters: Pruning percentage (e.g., 55%), number of qubits ($N$), and the fixed cardinality ($k$) for mask search.
main_assumptions: The held-out test split is only evaluated after the pruned structure is frozen, and the authors note that the search approach is a complement to, not a replacement for, quantum architecture search.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the ConQUESTA evaluation pipeline, compare search results against simple baselines (TABLE III), and show the massive combinatorial growth of raw mask space versus the controlled growth of evaluated masks (Fig. 3).
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, details the ConQUESTA framework combining saliency and cost, compares its joint-mask search against one-shot and simple baselines across multiple datasets, and concludes with scalability analysis.
why_interesting: While focused on ML, the core challenge of optimizing quantum circuits for physical hardware constraints (gate count, connectivity) is highly relevant to designing efficient quantum algorithms and simulating complex quantum systems on near-term devices.

Figure 3 isolates the combinatorial effect in a controlled synthetic dense-CRY fixed-k = 4 probe; it is not a fixed-ratio application benchmark. Raw prunable entanglers grow from N = 12 to 132, so the full mask space grows from 495 to 12,082,785 (24,400× increase). Screening caps K at 20 from 6 qubits onward, while unique evaluated masks grow only from 189 to 305 (1.62× increase). Consequently, the explored fraction falls from 38.18% to 0.0025%. Search time grows from 265 to 3254 s and time per unique mask from 1.40 to 10.66 s, showing that screening suppresses combinatorial growth while per-mask compilation becomes the next bottleneck.
